It was the first such event for The 50 in South America, where some of the world's most respected chefs came together to celebrate excellence in gastronomy around the globe.\

In Texas, even election night ends at Whataburger. James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, who will serve as senator and governor, toasted with fountain drinks, and honestly, the orange-and-white cups fit the occasion. The chain has long been where Texans go after the game, before heading home, or when they’re not quite ready to call it a night.\
\
@gabehiatt writes about the burgers, the Fancy Ketchup, and a Texas institution that’s bigger than politics at the link in bio.\

⁠\

When new hires at Weil, Gotshal & Manges gathered for orientation last week, senior lawyers at the legendary Wall Street firm—which burnished its reputation by leading mega-bankruptcies at Enron and Lehman Brothers—spoke of plans for a long and successful future.⁠\
⁠\
Nine days later, at 3:30 p.m. on Wednesday, senior partners gathered everyone again. This time, they had a different message: the 95-year-old firm was shutting down.⁠\
⁠\
“Given the significant partner departures, resulting loss of revenue and other disruptions, and after careful consideration of the alternatives, we have reached the heartbreaking conclusion that we must recommend an orderly dissolution of Weil, Gotshal & Manges,” said Barry Wolf, the firm’s leader, according to a video of the call reviewed by The Wall Street Journal. “This is not a recommendation we ever imagined making.”⁠\
⁠\
A rapid chain of events had led to a once-unthinkable outcome: The collapse virtually overnight of a venerated and profitable law firm with some 1,200 attorneys worldwide and more than $2 billion in revenue. Late last week, when merger talks collapsed and another slew of top partners chose to leave the firm, the writing was on the wall. Just five days later, Weil’s downfall was complete.⁠\
⁠\
Weil, the firm that invented much of modern bankruptcy practice and spent years as a go-to adviser for corporations under duress, turned that expertise on itself. It is now working with restructuring advisers of its own and figuring out how to engineer the kind of wind down it has done for clients for nearly a century since it was founded by top Jewish lawyers excluded from other elite shops.⁠\
⁠\
The idea that a run on top talent could take down even a leading firm in a matter of weeks has sent a shudder across the legal industry.⁠\
⁠\
Read more at the link in our bio.⁠\
⁠\
Photo: Marcin Golba\/Getty Images

Three American servicemembers were killed in a July 17 Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in the Jordanian desert. Satellite imagery shows the nighttime attack damaged at least 19 buildings where troops sleep.⁠\
⁠\
It was one of the deadliest nights of the war for U.S. forces. But it wasn’t the only attack targeting American troops where they live and sleep. That same week, Iran hit multiple housing units at other U.S. military installations across the region.⁠\
⁠\
The July strikes marked an alarming shift in Iran’s tactics and revealed an improvement in the regime’s ability to sequence attacks and hit targets with precision. Iran was taking more direct aim at the buildings that house American troops, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis of satellite data, Iranian military statements and interviews with U.S. officials.⁠\
⁠\
In all, the Journal found 274 structures at 24 installations across the Middle East that showed damage during the war’s first six months.⁠\
⁠\
Iran has hit America’s installations hard. Now, with President Trump considering a new wave of attacks on Iran, the U.S. military pulled some personnel off several of those locations ahead of possible retaliation, the Journal has reported. This comes as Pentagon officials worry that the regime has conserved some of its most sophisticated missiles and could improve its attacks in the next round of fighting.⁠\
⁠\
The latest cost estimate of the Iran war stands at $47.1 billion as of Oct. 16, according to a document viewed by the Journal. That doesn’t include damage to bases, which the Pentagon separately priced at a minimum of $5 billion, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter. That number could potentially be as high as $15 billion, according to a separate person briefed on the cost.⁠\
⁠\
The Defense Department and U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, declined to comment.⁠\
⁠\
At the link in our bio, see our analysis, the most comprehensive public accounting of the destruction to date.⁠\
⁠\
Satellite and other images: European Space Agency, Planet Labs, Airbus, Google Earth
